---
title: "From a Function to Two Inputs"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

One machine triples one input. What if a machine accepts two inputs and changes both at the same time?

## Build the intuition

A scalar function takes one number to another. A vector transformation accepts a coordinate pair and produces another pair. Linear algebra generalises familiar functions.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
T(x,y)=(2x+y,\ x-y)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** T is a transformation; (x,y) is a two-number input vector; 2x+y is the first output coordinate; x−y is the second output coordinate.

**Substitute real numbers:** Take input (x,y)=(3,2). The first output is 2×3+2=8; the second is 3−2=1; so T(3,2)=(8,1).

## Why the relationship is true

The same rule works for every input pair. The two outputs can be rewritten as combinations of the input components; later this becomes a matrix.

## Where the shortcut stops working

Not every function of vectors is linear. Adding a constant, such as T(x,y)=(2x+1,y), fails the fundamental linearity test T(0)=0.

## Your turn

Find T(1,0), T(0,1), then combine them to predict T(3,2).

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Math fundamentals, §§1.4, 1.8, 1.13. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
